filename: Senior Living Research Digest — Vision Loss — July 2026.md
title: Senior Living Research Digest — Vision Loss — July 2026
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Visual Noise Through Smart Glasses Improves Sight for People With Macular Degeneration
studies.the_study: Researchers tested whether adding controlled visual "noise" through augmented reality glasses could improve vision in people with wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Twelve adults with AMD in both eyes wore AR headsets that projected subtle visual static while reading a standard eye chart. The technique, called stochastic resonance, produced an immediate improvement of about 2.5 letters on the eye chart at optimal noise levels—without any training required. Healthy older adults (N=17) also showed improvement of about 2 letters.
studies.why_it_matters: Current treatments for wet AMD involve repeated eye injections that don't work for everyone. This non-invasive approach could offer a practical, wearable solution to help people see better in daily life.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have macular degeneration, new technology may eventually help you read and see more clearly using special glasses—no injections or surgery involved. Ask your eye doctor about emerging low-vision aids and clinical trials for AR-based devices.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities should monitor developments in wearable vision technology. AR-based visual aids could become valuable tools for residents with AMD, potentially improving independence in reading, recognizing faces, and navigating spaces.
studies.caveats: Small sample size (12 AMD participants); single testing session without long-term follow-up; technology not yet commercially available.

studies.title: Light Therapy Shows Promise for Slowing Early Macular Degeneration in Year-Long Trial
studies.the_study: In a 12-month randomized controlled trial across multiple centers, 138 eyes from 78 patients with early or intermediate dry AMD received either photobiomodulation (PBM)—a low-level light therapy—or a sham treatment. The PBM group showed significant reduction in drusen volume (fatty deposits under the retina that indicate AMD progression) and gained about 1.3 letters of visual acuity on average, while the sham group lost about 2.6 letters. Four eyes in the sham group developed the more severe "wet" form of AMD; none in the treatment group did.
studies.why_it_matters: There are currently no approved treatments to slow early or intermediate dry AMD. This light-based therapy, if validated in larger trials, could offer the first non-invasive option to preserve vision in the earliest stages of this common age-related condition.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've been told you have early macular degeneration with no treatment options, ask your eye specialist about emerging therapies like photobiomodulation. While not yet standard care, staying informed about clinical trials could open doors to new options.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Eye care coordinators in senior living settings should track developments in AMD treatment. Early-stage interventions could significantly reduce the number of residents who progress to vision-impairing advanced disease.
studies.caveats: Moderate sample size; 12-month follow-up may not capture long-term durability; some authors disclosed honoraria from companies in this field.

studies.title: Visual Hallucinations From Vision Loss Linked to Falls in Older Adults
studies.the_study: Researchers interviewed 17 older adults (average age 76) living with Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS)—visual hallucinations that can occur after vision loss—along with 12 healthcare professionals. Participants described how vivid, realistic hallucinations distracted them from actual hazards while walking, triggered automatic reactions that threw off balance, and sometimes completely obscured real surroundings. Falls occurred when hallucinations competed with attention needed to navigate safely.
studies.why_it_matters: CBS is underrecognized and rarely discussed, yet it adds a hidden layer of fall risk for people with vision loss. Understanding this connection could prevent injuries and improve quality of life.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you see things you know aren't real since your vision declined, you're not alone—this is called Charles Bonnet syndrome, and it can increase fall risk. Tell your doctor and consider strategies like better lighting and engaging activities that can reduce episodes.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Falls prevention programs in senior living should screen for visual hallucinations in residents with vision loss. Staff training on CBS can help identify at-risk residents and implement environmental modifications to reduce fall hazards.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample; findings describe experiences rather than measure fall rates; UK-based participants may not generalize to all populations.

studies.title: Unrecognized Vision Loss Often Overlooked by Older Adults Focused on Other Health Challenges
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted home visits and interviews with 15 Danish adults aged 75 and older who had been identified with vision loss through a home-based screening program but had not previously sought eye care. Despite clinical evidence of impaired vision—often from treatable eye disease—many participants didn't recognize or prioritize their vision problems. Other health challenges, caregiving responsibilities, and accumulated life hardships overshadowed vision concerns in their day-to-day priorities.
studies.why_it_matters: This research reveals why standard outreach may miss older adults who could benefit from eye care—their vision problems get lost amid competing demands and declining health.
studies.story_angle_primary: Even if your eyesight doesn't feel like your biggest concern right now, untreated vision problems can make other aspects of daily life harder. Consider accepting vision screenings offered during home visits—catching problems early gives you more options.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Home health workers and family caregivers should gently raise vision concerns with older adults, recognizing that competing health priorities may cause them to dismiss or minimize sight problems. Integrating vision screening into routine home care visits may catch treatable conditions.
studies.caveats: Small sample from one region of Denmark; qualitative design explores experiences rather than measuring outcomes; participants were already receiving home care services.

studies.title: Transient Vision Loss Signals Elevated Heart Attack and Stroke Risk for Years
studies.the_study: Using a research network of over 75,500 matched patients, researchers found that people who experienced transient vision loss (temporary blindness or dimming in one or both eyes) faced dramatically elevated cardiovascular risks. Within 14 days, stroke risk was 21 times higher and heart attack risk 5 times higher compared to matched controls. Even among those who remained event-free for a year, elevated risks for stroke and heart problems persisted for up to 10 years.
studies.why_it_matters: A brief episode of vision loss that resolves on its own is often a warning sign of serious cardiovascular disease—and the danger doesn't end after the initial weeks.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you experience sudden vision loss that clears up on its own, don't dismiss it—seek medical attention promptly. This can be an early warning of stroke or heart problems, and quick evaluation may prevent a more serious event.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living staff and family members should treat any report of temporary vision loss as a medical urgency requiring immediate cardiovascular workup. Long-term monitoring for heart health should continue even if initial tests are normal.
studies.caveats: Retrospective observational design cannot prove causation; control group had dry eye syndrome rather than no eye conditions; database study may have coding inconsistencies.

studies.title: Anti-VEGF Injections for Diabetic Eye Disease: Patients Describe Hope and Anxiety
studies.the_study: Researchers conducted interviews at 4 and 12 months with people with diabetes receiving regular eye injections (anti-VEGF therapy) for diabetic macular edema, a leading cause of vision loss in diabetes. Patients described an emotional journey of "health, hope, and worry"—experiencing physical discomfort, anxiety about outcomes, and varying degrees of visual improvement. Trust in healthcare providers and consistent communication were crucial for managing the emotional burden of ongoing treatment.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding the patient experience can help healthcare teams provide better support and improve treatment adherence for this chronic, often indefinite therapy.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're receiving eye injections for diabetic eye disease, know that feeling anxious or uncertain is normal. Don't hesitate to ask your care team questions and express concerns—good communication can make the experience more manageable.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Diabetes care teams and senior living health coordinators should recognize the emotional toll of repeated eye injections. Providing consistent providers, adequate information, and empathetic communication can help residents stick with treatment and cope with uncertainty.
studies.caveats: Qualitative study capturing experiences rather than measuring outcomes; small sample from Sweden may not generalize to all healthcare settings.

studies.title: Childhood Adversity Linked to Later-Life Cognitive Problems Through Vision Loss and Depression
studies.the_study: Analyzing data from over 20,000 Chinese adults aged 40 and older, researchers examined how 11 types of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) affect cognitive function in later life. Physical neglect and parental divorce or death were linked to worse cognition through pathways including less education, depression, and untreated vision loss. Emotional abuse and community violence showed direct negative associations with later-life thinking skills.
studies.why_it_matters: This research identifies treatable factors—including vision loss—as potential intervention points for reducing dementia risk in people who experienced childhood adversity.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you experienced difficult circumstances in childhood and are concerned about memory as you age, know that addressing current health issues—including getting your vision checked and treating depression—may help protect your thinking abilities.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Healthcare providers working with older adults should consider adverse childhood experiences as a risk marker for cognitive decline. Ensuring access to vision care, mental health services, and education may help interrupt pathways from early adversity to later dementia.
studies.caveats: Observational study cannot prove treating vision loss prevents cognitive decline; data from China may not generalize to other populations; self-reported childhood experiences subject to recall bias.

studies.title: Nearly Half of Dementia Cases in Turkey Potentially Preventable Through Lifestyle Changes
studies.the_study: Using Turkey's nationally representative health survey data, researchers calculated that 49.9% of dementia cases could theoretically be prevented by addressing 14 modifiable risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission. Physical inactivity, social isolation, and low education were the largest contributors. Women had a higher preventable fraction (54.2%) than men (44.3%), driven by differences in physical activity, depression, and social isolation. Untreated vision loss was also among the identified risk factors.
studies.why_it_matters: This analysis provides a roadmap for dementia prevention efforts, highlighting which factors—including sensory health—deserve attention in public health initiatives.
studies.story_angle_primary: Staying physically active, maintaining social connections, and getting your hearing and vision treated aren't just about quality of life today—they may help protect your brain health as you age.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities can position themselves as dementia prevention environments by prioritizing physical activity programming, social engagement opportunities, and ensuring residents have access to vision and hearing care.
studies.caveats: Population attributable fractions estimate theoretical maximum prevention assuming complete elimination of risk factors; observational data cannot prove interventions will reduce dementia rates.

studies.title: Dementia Risk Factors Vary Widely Across Countries, But Patterns Suggest Shared Prevention Strategies
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed harmonized data from over 214,000 adults aged 50+ across 14 countries and regions, examining 12 established dementia risk factors. While prevalence varied dramatically—low education affected 85.6% of older adults in China versus 12% in the US, for example—similar clusters of risk factors emerged across settings. More than half of people in every country had at least two risk factors. Vision loss was among the social and sensory factors that commonly clustered together.
studies.why_it_matters: Despite cultural and economic differences, common patterns in how risk factors group together could guide the design of dementia prevention programs that work across diverse populations.
studies.story_angle_primary: Regardless of where you live, addressing multiple risk factors together—such as staying socially connected, treating hearing and vision problems, and managing heart health—may offer the best protection against cognitive decline.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living operators developing programming for diverse resident populations can draw on evidence that certain risk factor clusters appear across cultures, suggesting that comprehensive wellness approaches addressing cardiovascular, social, and sensory health may be universally beneficial.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional analysis provides snapshot rather than tracking changes over time; self-reported data for some risk factors; harmonization across different surveys may introduce measurement inconsistencies.

studies.title: Gut Bacteria May Influence Age-Related Macular Degeneration Progression
studies.the_study: This comprehensive review examines the emerging "gut-retina connection"—the relationship between intestinal bacteria and age-related macular degeneration. Age-related changes in gut microbiota (dysbiosis) appear to contribute to inflammation, altered immune responses, and metabolic changes that may accelerate retinal damage. The authors reviewed evidence from animal studies and early human research suggesting that interventions targeting gut health—including probiotics, dietary changes, and fecal transplantation—might help prevent or slow AMD progression.
studies.why_it_matters: If confirmed in clinical trials, addressing gut health could offer a new avenue for preventing vision loss from AMD, potentially through dietary modifications or supplements.
studies.story_angle_primary: While it's too early for specific recommendations, the connection between gut health and eye health is an active area of research. Maintaining a healthy, fiber-rich diet that supports beneficial gut bacteria may have benefits beyond digestion.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living dining programs focused on gut-healthy foods (high fiber, fermented foods, diverse plant-based options) may support multiple aspects of resident health, including potentially eye health, though direct evidence for AMD prevention in humans is still developing.
studies.caveats: Review article synthesizing mostly animal and preclinical research; human clinical trials needed before dietary interventions can be recommended for AMD prevention.

studies.title: Global Vision Loss Burden Growing as Populations Age, With Disparities Across Regions
studies.the_study: Analyzing data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021, researchers found that while age-standardized rates of blindness remained stable from 1990 to 2021, the absolute number of affected people is growing as populations age. In 2021, Southern sub-Saharan Africa had the highest prevalence rates, while South Asia had the highest disability burden. Cataract-related disability from household air pollution decreased by 38.4% over the study period. Projections suggest the burden will continue growing through 2050.
studies.why_it_matters: These findings highlight where global eye health resources are most needed and underscore the importance of preparing healthcare systems for increasing vision care demands as populations age.
studies.story_angle_primary: Vision problems are increasingly common as we age, but many causes are treatable. Regular eye exams become more important with each passing decade—don't wait for noticeable problems to get checked.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living organizations should anticipate growing demand for vision-related services and accommodations. Planning for residents with visual impairments—including lighting, wayfinding, and activity adaptations—will become increasingly important.
studies.caveats: Estimates rely on modeling and may not capture recent improvements in some regions; projections assume current trends continue; regional data quality varies.

studies.title: Inherited Retinal Diseases Affect Over 60 Per 100,000 People in Sweden
studies.the_study: Using Sweden's comprehensive national health registers from 2006-2021, researchers identified 6,544 people living with inherited retinal diseases (IRDs)—genetic conditions causing progressive vision loss. The overall prevalence was 62.6 per 100,000 people, with an incidence rate of 3.4 new cases per 100,000 per year that remained stable over two decades. Retinitis pigmentosa-like conditions were the most common specified subtype.
studies.why_it_matters: This first comprehensive national estimate of IRD burden provides baseline data for healthcare planning and highlights the population affected by emerging gene therapies.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or a family member has been diagnosed with an inherited eye condition, know that these diseases are increasingly well-documented and gene therapy options are becoming available. Genetic counseling can help families understand inheritance patterns and treatment possibilities.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities may encounter residents with IRDs who face unique challenges as their vision progressively declines. Understanding that these are genetic, often slowly progressive conditions can inform appropriate support and accommodation planning.
studies.caveats: Study funded partly by Johnson & Johnson through research collaboration; may underestimate cases not captured in healthcare registers; Swedish population may not generalize globally.

studies.title: Communication Challenges Compound the Burden of Inherited Vision Loss
studies.the_study: Researchers interviewed 16 people aged 20-69 with inherited retinal diseases and 5 family members about their experiences communicating about their condition. Five key themes emerged: challenges with healthcare provider communication, personal barriers to accepting the diagnosis, complex family dynamics around a shared genetic condition, others' misconceptions about vision loss as a spectrum, and difficult decisions about when and how to disclose their condition to others.
studies.why_it_matters: Beyond the visual impairment itself, people with progressive vision loss face significant communication barriers that can affect their mental health, relationships, and access to appropriate support.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're struggling to explain your vision condition to family, friends, or employers, you're not alone. Many people with progressive vision loss find these conversations difficult. Consider asking your eye care team about counseling resources or support groups.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living staff should understand that vision loss exists on a spectrum and may not be obvious. Residents with inherited eye conditions may need support navigating disclosure decisions and may benefit from accessible mental health services.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample; age range included younger adults, not exclusively seniors; Australian participants may have different experiences than those in other healthcare systems.

studies.title: Hearing and Vision Support for People With Dementia Shows Promise in European Trial
studies.the_study: The SENSE-Cog trial enrolled 252 pairs of people with dementia and their care partners across Europe, testing an 18-week home-based intervention to address hearing and vision problems. Among those in the active treatment group, 81% of those assessed for hearing loss were prescribed hearing aids with acceptable adherence. People with more severe cognitive impairment received more intensive support, suggesting the intervention was appropriately tailored. Care partners played a central role in supporting sensory health improvements.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing and vision problems are often overlooked in people with dementia, yet addressing them may improve quality of life. This study demonstrates that sensory interventions are feasible even for people with cognitive impairment.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you or someone you care for has both dementia and hearing or vision problems, know that addressing sensory issues is still worthwhile and achievable. Ask healthcare providers about hearing aid fittings and vision assessments even when memory problems are present.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Memory care settings should prioritize sensory assessments and support for residents. This trial shows that hearing aid adherence is achievable in people with dementia when care partners are engaged, and more intensive support may be needed for those with greater cognitive impairment.
studies.caveats: COVID-19 pandemic required protocol modifications; 40% of active arm participants did not complete all intervention components; study assessed feasibility and delivery rather than definitive efficacy.

studies.title: Gene Therapy Shows Greater Visual Recovery Than Current Treatment for Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy
studies.the_study: Researchers compared outcomes of lenadogene nolparvovec gene therapy versus idebenone (the only currently approved treatment) for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) caused by a specific genetic mutation. Using statistical methods to adjust for differences between trial populations, gene therapy showed significantly higher rates of clinically relevant visual recovery at 24 months (60.4% vs 35.4% in one comparison; 69.5% vs 39.0% in another).
studies.why_it_matters: LHON is a rare genetic condition causing rapid, severe vision loss, primarily in young adults. These findings suggest gene therapy may offer substantially better outcomes than current standard treatment.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have a family member with LHON or carry the genetic mutation yourself, be aware that gene therapy options are emerging that may offer better visual outcomes than existing treatments. Discuss genetic testing and treatment options with a specialist.
studies.story_angle_secondary: While LHON typically affects younger people, older adults may have children or grandchildren diagnosed with this condition. Awareness of advancing treatment options can help families navigate difficult conversations about prognosis and emerging therapies.
studies.caveats: Indirect comparison between different trials rather than head-to-head study; several authors are consultants for or employed by the gene therapy manufacturer; treatment requires specialized center access.

studies.title: Higher Virus Levels in the Eye Predict Worse Vision Outcomes in Acute Retinal Necrosis
studies.the_study: In the largest single-center study of acute retinal necrosis (ARN)—a rare but severe viral infection of the retina—researchers reviewed 148 cases treated over 36 years. Varicella-zoster virus (the chickenpox/shingles virus) caused 84.5% of cases. Higher viral DNA levels in eye fluid at diagnosis and greater extent of retinal damage both predicted worse final vision. Average vision worsened significantly from presentation to final follow-up despite treatment.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding which patients are at highest risk for poor outcomes could help guide treatment intensity and help patients and families set realistic expectations.
studies.story_angle_primary: Sudden vision loss with eye redness and pain requires immediate medical attention—it could be a viral infection of the retina that needs urgent treatment. The shingles vaccine may help prevent some cases of this condition.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living health staff should recognize that sudden, painful vision loss is a medical emergency. Prompt referral to ophthalmology and initiation of antiviral treatment may improve outcomes, particularly when viral load testing can guide care intensity.
studies.caveats: Retrospective single-center study; quantitative viral load data available for only 49% of patients; cases span 36 years during which treatment approaches evolved.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Multiple studies in this batch converge on vision loss as a modifiable risk factor for dementia and cognitive decline—not merely a quality-of-life issue but a brain health concern. Study #7 (PMID 42371784) identifies untreated vision loss as a pathway linking childhood adversity to later-life cognitive problems. Study #8 (PMID 40583126) includes vision loss among 14 modifiable dementia risk factors in Turkey. Study #9 (PMID 42437564) shows vision loss clustering with other social and sensory risk factors across 14 countries. Study #14 (PMID 42212629) demonstrates that addressing vision (and hearing) problems in people with dementia is feasible and may improve outcomes.

**Why pitch this now:** The Lancet Commission's inclusion of vision loss as a dementia risk factor is gaining empirical traction across diverse populations, yet public awareness lags far behind. Most older adults and caregivers still think of vision care and brain health as separate domains.

**Angle:** A feature titled "Your Eyes and Your Brain: The Surprising Link Between Vision Care and Dementia Prevention" could synthesize this emerging evidence for older adults and senior living professionals, making the case that routine eye exams and timely treatment aren't just about seeing better—they may be protecting cognitive function. The piece could include practical guidance on integrating vision screening into dementia prevention strategies.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — Vision Loss — July 2026
**Checked:** 2026-07-13 | **Studies reviewed:** 16
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

### Study 1: Visual Noise Through Smart Glasses Improves Sight for People With Macular Degeneration
**PMID:** 42014412 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. Sample sizes (N=12 AMD, N=17 healthy), improvement figures (~2.5 letters for AMD, ~2 letters for healthy), study design, and the immediate/no-training nature of results all match. Caveats appropriately note the small sample and single session.

---

### Study 2: Light Therapy Shows Promise for Slowing Early Macular Degeneration in Year-Long Trial
**PMID:** 42259594 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Imprecise visual acuity gain/loss figures** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "gained about 1.3 letters of visual acuity on average, while the sham group lost about 2.6 letters"
- **Abstract says:** "+1.31 ± 6.7 letters" and "-2.62±7.1 letters"
- **Problem:** The digest rounds correctly but omits the large standard deviations, which are important context for understanding variability.
- **Suggested fix:** No change required, but could add "(with wide individual variation)" if space permits.

**Issue B. Conversion rate to wet AMD slightly imprecise** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Four eyes in the sham group developed the more severe 'wet' form of AMD; none in the treatment group did."
- **Abstract says:** "Four eyes in the sham group developed macular neovascularisation, compared with none in the PBM group (p=0.044)"
- **Problem:** "Macular neovascularisation" is technically the term used; "wet AMD" is an acceptable lay translation. No substantive error.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

---

### Study 3: Visual Hallucinations From Vision Loss Linked to Falls in Older Adults
**PMID:** 42143601 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample size (17 older adults with CBS, 12 professionals), mean age (76 years), qualitative design, and key findings about falls mechanisms all match the abstract. Caveats appropriately note the qualitative nature and UK setting.

---

### Study 4: Unrecognized Vision Loss Often Overlooked by Older Adults Focused on Other Health Challenges
**PMID:** 42271249 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample size (15 participants, plus observations), age criterion (≥75), Danish setting, qualitative design, and key themes about competing priorities all match. Caveats appropriately note the regional and qualitative limitations.

---

### Study 5: Transient Vision Loss Signals Elevated Heart Attack and Stroke Risk for Years
**PMID:** 42365525 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sample size description** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "over 75,500 matched patients"
- **Abstract says:** "37 750 patients were included in each cohort" (totaling 75,500)
- **Problem:** "Over 75,500" is slightly imprecise; the actual total is exactly 75,500 (37,750 × 2).
- **Suggested fix:** "75,500 matched patients (37,750 in each group)"

All other statistics (21-fold stroke risk, 5-fold MI risk at 14 days, 10-year persistence) match the abstract accurately.

---

### Study 6: Anti-VEGF Injections for Diabetic Eye Disease: Patients Describe Hope and Anxiety
**PMID:** 42008767 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Country of origin not mentioned in digest body** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Caveats mention "small sample from Sweden"
- **Abstract says:** Institutions listed are in Sweden (Uppsala University, Dalarna University)
- **Problem:** The digest correctly identifies Sweden in caveats but doesn't specify sample size. Abstract doesn't provide N.
- **Suggested fix:** Caveat could note "Sample size not specified in abstract; conducted in Sweden."

**Issue B. Sample size unverifiable** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "small sample from Sweden"
- **Abstract says:** No specific N provided
- **Problem:** "Small" is reasonable for a qualitative longitudinal study but unverifiable from abstract.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sample size not reported; qualitative study from Sweden"

---

### Study 7: Childhood Adversity Linked to Later-Life Cognitive Problems Through Vision Loss and Depression
**PMID:** 42371784 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Sample size rounding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "over 20,000 Chinese adults"
- **Abstract says:** "20,010 adults"
- **Problem:** Slight imprecision; "over 20,000" technically accurate but could be more precise.
- **Suggested fix:** "20,010 Chinese adults" or "approximately 20,000"

**Issue B. Age criterion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "aged 40 and older"
- **Abstract says:** "aged 40 years or more"
- **Problem:** Accurate match.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

---

### Study 8: Nearly Half of Dementia Cases in Turkey Potentially Preventable Through Lifestyle Changes
**PMID:** 40583126 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The 49.9% overall PAF, gender breakdown (54.2% women, 44.3% men), 14 risk factors from Lancet Commission framework, and key contributors (physical inactivity, social isolation, low education) all match. Caveats appropriately note the theoretical nature of PAF calculations.

---

### Study 9: Dementia Risk Factors Vary Widely Across Countries, But Patterns Suggest Shared Prevention Strategies
**PMID:** 42437564 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample size (214,251 → digest says "over 214,000"), 14 countries/regions, 12 risk factors, specific prevalence examples (85.6% low education in China vs 12% in US), and the >50% with ≥2 risk factors finding all match accurately. Caveats appropriately note cross-sectional limitations.

---

### Study 10: Gut Bacteria May Influence Age-Related Macular Degeneration Progression
**PMID:** 41759744 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The digest accurately describes this as a review article, correctly identifies the gut-retina connection concept, mentions preclinical/animal evidence, and appropriately frames potential interventions (probiotics, diet, fecal transplantation) as areas of research rather than proven treatments. Caveats properly note the need for human clinical trials.

---

### Study 11: Global Vision Loss Burden Growing as Populations Age, With Disparities Across Regions
**PMID:** 41224521 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The GBD 2021 data source, 1990-2021 timeframe, projections to 2050, Southern sub-Saharan Africa having highest prevalence, South Asia having highest DALY burden, and the 38.4% decrease in cataract DALYs from household air pollution all match the abstract precisely.

---

### Study 12: Inherited Retinal Diseases Affect Over 60 Per 100,000 People in Sweden
**PMID:** 42431723 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Incidence rate stability claim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "incidence rate of 3.4 new cases per 100,000 per year that remained stable over two decades"
- **Abstract says:** "estimating an overall average incidence rate of 3.4/100 000 individuals/year" and conclusion states "stable incidence of IRD over the past two decades"
- **Problem:** Accurate match.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

**Issue B. Funding disclosure adequately captured** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Caveats mention "Study funded partly by Johnson & Johnson through research collaboration"
- **Abstract says:** Authors disclose employment at Johnson & Johnson and grant funding from Johnson & Johnson through research collaboration
- **Problem:** The caveat captures this appropriately.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

---

### Study 13: Communication Challenges Compound the Burden of Inherited Vision Loss
**PMID:** 42149821 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample sizes (16 individuals with IRDs, 5 family members), age range (20-69), five key themes, and Australian setting all match. Caveats appropriately note the age range includes younger adults and the Australian healthcare context.

---

### Study 14: Hearing and Vision Support for People With Dementia Shows Promise in European Trial
**PMID:** 42212629 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Hearing aid prescription rate denominator** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "81% of those assessed for hearing loss were prescribed hearing aids"
- **Abstract says:** "Of 124 assessed for hearing loss, 101 (81%) were prescribed hearing aids"
- **Problem:** Accurate match.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

**Issue B. Completion rate** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "40% of active arm participants did not complete all intervention components"
- **Abstract says:** "fidelity-completion of all primary components-was 60% (75/124)"
- **Problem:** The digest correctly calculates 40% non-completion (100% - 60% = 40%). Accurate.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

---

### Study 15: Gene Therapy Shows Greater Visual Recovery Than Current Treatment for Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy
**PMID:** 42019972 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The comparison method (MAIC), treatment names (lenadogene nolparvovec vs idebenone), recovery rates (60.4% vs 35.4%; 69.5% vs 39.0%), 24-month timepoint, and the specific mutation (m.11778G>A MT-ND4) all match. Caveats appropriately note the indirect comparison design and author conflicts of interest.

---

### Study 16: Higher Virus Levels in the Eye Predict Worse Vision Outcomes in Acute Retinal Necrosis
**PMID:** 41986092 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Viral load data availability** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Caveats state "quantitative viral load data available for only 49% of patients"
- **Abstract says:** "Quantitative aqueous viral-load data were available in 73 of 148 patients" (49.3%)
- **Problem:** Accurate calculation and appropriate caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** None required.

**Issue B. Timespan of cases** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "148 cases treated over 36 years"
- **Abstract says:** "1985-2021" (36 years)
- **Problem:** Accurate match.
